correctness.rationale: On both arcs h± conjugates the base to translation, and the skew term goes to zero at the fixed endpoints. Interpolating the translation and the vertical term gives an isotopy by homeomorphisms. Each point of an open arc has a neighborhood inside a translation strip of width <1, hence is wandering; both endpoint fibers are fixed. The lift of the base fixes the endpoints of each interval, giving bounded horizontal displacement. In the other coordinate, sin(2π(s+j)) is constant along the orbit and the sum of the amplitudes is uniformly Oβ(n^(1−β)), by ordering the negative tail by increasing distance from the cutoff. This proves uniform convergence of the normalized lift displacement to zero. For entropy, the same sum estimate and summability of the tail derivative bound the Lipschitz constants of ALL partial Birkhoff sums by Oβ(n^(1−β)) on each unit strip, including across the continuous piecewise-smooth cutoff. A mesh at that inverse scale suffices for each of O(n) central strips. On the far negative tail the base trajectories all stay near r for large n. At fixed fractional mesh coordinate u, all amplitude differences between two strips have the same sign at every time (and the sine factor is fixed), so the largest partial-sum difference is the endpoint difference. Binning those endpoint values gives O(n^(1−β)) additional choices per u and hence O(n^(2−2β)) there; changing u to its mesh point uses the uniform Lipschitz bound. The positive tail and fixed circles cost O(1), and the zero-cocycle second arc costs O(n). The spanning bound O(n^(2−β)) also proves zero topological entropy. For the lower bound, Ω(n) separated transit times j in [n/3,2n/3] are detected at time j by the base coordinate; h+(u) for u∈[0,1/8] stays uniformly away from either endpoint. Within each transit strip, until k=floor(j/2) all amplitudes are on the increasing negative tail and of order n^(−β). Differentiation over u∈[0,1/8] gives ∂u B_k≥cβ n^(1−β). Thus a mesh of spacing K n^(β−1) produces endpoint lift differences >4ε. Differences increase in time and the one-step increments are <ε for large n, so a first crossing of ε gives a difference in (ε,2ε], genuine circle separation before k<n. These two separations give Ω(n^(2−β)) at fixed small ε and the required exponent. The argument is for each real 0<β<1, not merely sampled parameters. The frozen script was inspected only; no numerical simulation is needed for the proof.
residual_risks: No endpoints β=0 or β=1, no regularity beyond continuity of the cocycle, and no claim of zero rotation vector for lifts other than the specified one. The fixed circles also rule out minimality.

evidence: Problem 1 asks for every α∈[1,∞], zero topological entropy, identity isotopy and a singleton for any lift. The Morse–Smale theorem assumes a Morse–Smale diffeomorphism of a compact surface. The frozen-base theorem concerns fiber translations over a fixed base, with exponent from its velocity image.
broader_coverage.reasoning: An open question is not coverage; this finding resolves its open subinterval (1,2). The two pointwise fixed circles place the example outside the Morse–Smale hypotheses. The fixed-base velocity theorem cannot be specialized to a moving north–south base.

evidence: The zero-singleton example immediately before Problem 1 has positive topological entropy. A rational base becomes the identity after iteration, a reduction explicitly used for the zero–one law; no positive iterate of the frozen g is the identity.

value.rationale: The result supplies an explicit continuum of intermediate growth exponents in the exact realization class posed in Corrêa's Problem 1. It separates sublinear unwrapped drift (hence zero rotation) from growth of distinguishable orbit segments and shows why a slowly decaying resonant term amplifies transit-strip complexity without giving positive topological entropy.
residual_risks: This is a partial solution in the exponent variable; no endpoints, exponent ≥2, smoothness, minimality or area-preserving realization are delivered.
